The board of transport commissioners is continuing to make progress with the freight rates equalization program. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these are all matters which are examined by the board of transport commissioners. I have reported to the hon. member the results which have been obtained so far from the examination that is being carried out, and I have given him a full answer to his question.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON EQUALIZATION PROGRAM

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence in view of his statement appearing at page 37 of Hansard for October 16, to the effect that in the training period for the non-permanent militia starting October 1 emphasis will be given to civil defence. May I ask the minister whether literature, directions for courses of study, equipment and instructions have been provided to the militia to carry on its training to date with emphasis on civil defence?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subtopic: REPORTED TRANSFER OF RESERVE ARMY TO CIVIL DEFENCE ROLE
speechtext:
The annual training instruction to which I referred described in general terms the type of training which was to be carried out by the militia in connection with the civil defence duties; in particular, it laid down that certain staff discussions would take place with civil authorities. It directed that study should be given to the application of corps training to civil defence requirements, and also that there should be mobile support group exercises. Beyond that, there has been a block syllabus of some 60 periods based on the civil defence precis which have been issued. Furthermore military publications dealing with first aid, traffic control and radiation monitoring have been issued. I think that covers in general the publications which have been issued. These will be followed up by further instruction as the training proceeds.
Regarding equipment, no special equipment has been issued as yet to army units. This matter is under consideration with the civil defence authorities, who in the past have been responsible for the issue of such equipment.
A large number of militia officers have attended the civil defence college at Arnprior over a considerable period of time. It is hoped that it will be possible to step up the attendance at these courses by other militia officers, non-commissioned officers and men.

Yesterday the hon. member for Comox-Al-berni (Mr. Barnett) asked the Minister of
Inquiries of the Ministry Fisheries whether he had taken any steps to terminate the investigation into the affairs of the united fishermen and allied workers' union of British Columbia by the combines investigation branch. The Minister of Fisheries promised a reply today, and since the combines branch is under my department he asked me to reply.
The investigation referred to is an investigation into the production, purchase and sale of fish in the province of British Columbia, which was commenced by the director under the Combines Investigation Act as the result of a formal complaint under the act. The matter has been the subject of considerable previous discussion in the house, particularly between the hon. member who asked the question yesterday and my predecessor in the former government.
The position is that no steps have been taken by the minister to terminate the investigation because, under the present legislation, the minister has no authority to direct that an investigation be discontinued. The terms of the act require that the director in such a case as this:
. . . shall cause an inquiry to be made into all such matters as he considers necessary to inquire into with the view of determining the facts.
Such an inquiry then proceeds until, again in the words of the act:
. . . the director is of the opinion that the matter being inquired into does not justify further inquiry-
-or until the inquiry culminates in a written report by the restrictive trade practices commission to the minister. The minister himself, by the legislation, is given no authority to terminate the investigation.

May I say this to the minister. He has been in the house as long as I have been here, 22 years. He knows the rules of the house; he knows that a point of order should not be raised on a matter which is not before a court of record. That is my point, but I take his explanation. I thought he was trying to stop me from following up a matter which the government does not want brought before the house at this time.
Yesterday at the conclusion of my remarks I began to discuss the trans-Canada pipe line. I want to make it very clear that I am in favour-and so is my party-of transporting gas from the gas fields of Alberta, or anywhere else, to the users in eastern Canada or anywhere else, provided it is done in the public interest, in the interest of the consumers as well as in the interest of those who produce the gas wherever it may be found. We are in favour of that.
I raise the question of the trans-Canada pipe line today because that pipe line will remain the property of the people of Canada for a long period of time. It is being constructed, it is being paid for by the Canadian people and then leased. We objected to the lending of money to a private corporation to build the first leg of the pipe line as far as Winnipeg, and I think the government still has the right and should exercise it to expropriate that leg of the pipe line which the people of Canada financed. At the time the Conservative party agreed that the people of Canada were financing it for a private and very largely alien-controlled corporation.
The profits that accrue from that public utility should accrue to the people of Canada and not to any group of private promoters who, as late as February of 1957, were described by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) as "buccaneers". When he was somewhat taken to task in the house by the then minister of trade and commerce, Right Hon. C. D. Howe, he defined what he meant by "buccaneers" when he used the word. I find the definition he gave at page 1607 of Hansard of February 25, 1957, and it is in these words:
A buccaneer is one who reaps a piratical profit without any danger or fear to himself. It is in that sense that I use the expression.
But the present government apparently is quite content to allow men whom the Prime Minister described as buccaneers to reap a piratical profit. They have already reaped huge profits without any danger or fear to themselves.
I said last night that while I welcome the appointment of a royal commission 1 deplore the fact that it now appears quite evident

that the government's intentions and, indeed, the Conservative party's sincerity in June, 1956, can be questioned. Their whole attitude in that debate can be questioned unless they take action to prevent these buccaneers from reaping the profits that will accrue because of the expenditures made by the government and the people of Canada.
What did the Prime Minister say in that debate? He said a lot of things. I have the Hansards here. When he spoke in the debate on May 17, 1956, he said, as found at page 4032 of Hansard:
The perquisites here-
I think that must be a typographical error. I think the word should be "prerequisites" and not "perquisites". I continue:
-are that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should abdicate his belief in democratic principles and deny those in opposition the right to advance their arguments and to educate public opinion or to find out why there is such solicitude on the part of the members of this government. For five long years this pampered pet-
This is what the present Prime Minister said.
-Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, by deviation, by change of direction, by protestation, by alteration in course, has postponed that estimable end of securing a market for Alberta gas and the making available to other parts of Canada of that necessary form of energy. I ask the Prime Minister today to tell this house why he is so fearful of the facts; why he was afraid to allow the true facts of this nefarious scheme to be elucidated? I ask why he found it necessary, and the members of his government found it necessary, to muzzle the representatives of the people in advance of anything in the nature of a filibuster or an interference on the part of the opposition with the policy and program of the government. I ask him to explain that today, for certainly the day of silence is past. Are they afraid of the truth over there? Is that why they hide behind the caricature of parliament which they have substituted by the adoption of the parliamentary form of closure in a way that it has never been adopted before?
A caricature of parliament, a nefarious deal. I ask the government today if the Prime Minister stated the opinion of his party at that time when he said this was a nefarious deal. If he did state their opinion the facts which brought him to that opinion are facts that are there today; and if the facts are as he believed and indicated them to be, then the present government should not allow Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to operate the line across northern Ontario. Indeed, they should go further than that. They should restore to the people of Canada ownership and control of that portion of the pipe line which was alienated from the people of Canada by money provided by this parliament. That is their clear duty.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) spoke at some length regarding this same proposition. I am not going to quote him at 96698-10

I conclude my remarks by this statement, and I make it after careful consideration. I believe that this measure now proposed by the government is the greatest betrayal of the Canadian people since confederation.
What is he doing about it now? If he believes that this was the greatest betrayal of the Canadian people since confederation then he should restore to the people the utility with regard to which he says the former government betrayed the trust of the people of Canada. Well, it is a very short quotation and is to be found at page 3935 of Hansard of May 15, 1956. He referred to the trans-Canada pipe line as "this infamous proposal". Infamous proposal. Now the government is apparently quite content to go along with this nefarious deal, with this group of buccaneers, and to carry out this infamous plan, this infamous proposal. I say that if they do so there has never been a greater betrayal of the Canadian people by a government than the betrayal that the present government of Canada contemplates.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that one can question their sincerity. How they made the halls across this country ring. How television portrayed the Prime Minister denouncing the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines deal, denouncing the destruction of parliament because of the manner in which it was done. I say that unless they rectify the situation they will have done more to destroy parliament than even the previous government did, because they will have betrayed the trust that the people of Canada had in them when they elected them on June 10. Again, the Minister of Finance had this to say a little later, as found at page 4694 of Hansard of June 5, 1956:
Well, sir, it seems now we are narrowed down to a choice between two courses, the government's iniquitous proposal to hand over to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited great sums of public money to help them out and public construction of the entire line.
Apparently the present government is quite willing to go ahead and finance, by public money, the construction of the entire line in northern Ontario, which has just begun and which the present Minister of Finance described as an iniquitous proposal. He will be the minister controlling the finances of this country. He will make the necessary

The Address-Mr. Coldwell financial arrangements in order that the iniquitous proposal can be carried out. Was there anything more insincere than that?
Then the Prime Minister spoke on May 29, 1956, at page 4423 of Hansard for that date. He said:
What have you been doing for five long years? Playing around with this corporation, with these adventurers from Texas and New York trading away Canada's natural resources at the expense of the Canadian people.
This is the Prime Minister of the present government which has the power to prevent this being done. Are they going to use that power, or are they going to betray the Canadian people to the adventurers from Texas and New York, the buccaneers as the present Prime Minister called them on one occasion? At one time he referred to the pipe line proposal as "this ramshackle caricature of national development". Yet he and his colleagues have the nerve to set up a royal commission to inquire into this ramshackle caricature of national development, under the guise that this is part of the Conservative policy on national development which they tried, and probably successfully, to sell to the people of Canada prior to June 10.
There is another aspect of this with which I intended to deal last night. Perhaps I would not have put on the record today just what I have put on the record if it had not been for the interruptions in my address last evening. I am thinking of government action to prevent the promoters of pipe-line companies from making millions of dollars at the expense of the public of Canada. Of course, they have already made many millions of dollars by having allotted to them promotion shares, about which the people knew nothing and about which this parliament knew nothing, at prices that were so small. Perhaps it is already too late to catch the real culprits in this matter. Certainly it will be even later if the government waits for the many months or years it may take the royal commission to make its report.
Those of us who know the history of the North American continent remember that in the early years of the oil and railway industries the robber barons, as they called them, built up for themselves huge fortunes. We are allowing a few people in this country, and their friends across the line, to follow the examples of these robber barons. The government, which shared these views with me and those associated with me, are now in the seats of power and are apparently prepared to betray the Canadian people to these robber barons or these buccaneers, as the Prime Minister referred to them.

However, I am not going to argue with my hon. friend at the moment. I am arguing with the new government of Canada, so allow me to argue with them.
I want to take a look at a few of these people to whom reference was made in connection with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. There was another outfit which was headed by a gentleman named McMahon. Those of us who were in the house will remember the name McMahon. Mr. McMahon was to have been the chosen instrument of the Conservative party if some of their front bench members had had their way. I said at the time that I agreed that Mr. McMahon's operations certainly did not recommend him to parliament and the people of Canada. I think that is quite right. For example, let us see what he has done with the Westcoast Transmission Company. Let me say that when I first made these computations some months ago the results, of course, were very much higher than they were yesterday when the computations were revised, because there has been a significant fall in the stock market

during the last three months. However, even revising these figures at present stock prices, the profits made by Mr. McMahon and his associates are still enormous, just as the profits made by the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines interests were enormous. May I add that these shares were very largely unloaded at high prices on smaller investors in Canada and elsewhere. They have seen their investments diminish in value since.
I am quite happy that my colleagues, during last session, were able to prevent the splitting of the shares of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company because, had the company been able at that time to split the shares which were then worth $124 five ways, making them worth approximately $25 each, the people today would find they had shares valued at less than $12, because yesterday the shares were selling at $58. Hon. members will recall that the president of Westcoast Transmission was Mr. Frank McMahon, the favourite of the Conservative party in June, 1956. Mr. McMahon was in a very fortunate position throughout these operations. He was an insider. He was able to obtain the common stock of this company at a special price, indeed at only 5 cents- make no mistake-5 cents a share for stock that was offered to the public at $5 a share and which today is selling at $27.50.
He bought 155,000 shares at that price of 5 cents. These cost him in the neighbourhood of $7,700, and for that investment he acquired an equity worth over $4 million. I repeat, an investment of $7,700 at 5 cents a share brought $4 million of equity.
In addition the same Mr. McMahon, whom some members of the Conservative party would have brought into the picture in preference to Mr. Tanner and the gentleman from Texas, Mr. Coates, was granted options on 200,000 additional shares to be purchased at any time before January 31, 1960, at $6 per share. This stock is now selling, as I have said, for $27.50. In other words he could invest a part of the tremendous capital gain he has already made, even under present comparatively depressed prices, to realize a further capital gain today in excess of another $4 million. Surely it does not take a royal commission to establish the vicious exploitation by these robber barons of the Canadian people which is taking place in the gas and oil industry.
I say it is the duty of this parliament to protect the people of Canada from exploitation and raids of this description, and the present government has taken office because many of the people in Canada believed that 96698-10J
The Address-Mr. Caldwell this government would do just that. Now it is clearly prepared to betray the Canadian public in this regard.
This kind of thing is something that has happened in any pipe line company that one might name. I referred to the West-coast Transmission Company Limited. Mr. McMahon is not the only person to make tremendous capital gains on this company's stock. For an initial investment of something like $20 million the stockholders of this company acquired shares now worth $125 million, or a capital gain of $105 million. I will just mention also Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, which stock originally sold for $54 million and is already worth $124 million, or another capital gain of $80 million.

May I say this, and I want to make this very clear. I am not opposed to persons who invest risk capital getting a return for the risk they take. That stock was sold for about $1 million and it is now worth $24 million, or a capital gain of $23 million. I could go on; there are the Union Gas Company of Ontario, Consumers Gas Company of Toronto, Northern Ontario Natural Gas, which hold

franchises throughout northern Ontario, and what has been done in that connection will not bear examination.
Just taking the six companies I have mentioned there is a total original investment of $148 million now worth $598 million or nearly $600 million. The point I am making is this, that this has been made possible not by those people, in the main, taking all the risk, but because Canada took the risk. Canada, in part, put up the money for the initial steps and the present government of Canada is going to put up the money to build the pipe line for them all across northern Canada. They will reap any profits that accrue from the flow of gas in that pipe line.
We can be sure that taking the other companies into account, there have been capital gains of more than half a billion dollars. I could go on of course to elaborate further, but I say to the government, surely this is something that calls for immediate action, particularly in view of their record in the house during the pipe-line debates of 1956. Instead of any kind of equivocation or abdication of responsibility properly theirs, and which they assumed when they so bitterly opposed the Trans-Canada Pipe Line deal in 1956, I say that action should be taken now to stop the carrying out of the deal as far as we are able to do so.
Second, it is about time the government of Canada instituted a capital gains tax. A capital gains tax would bring back to the people of Canada some of those immense speculative profits, as well, of course, as bringing the pipe-line companies over which we have jurisdiction under public ownership and control. These are, after all, public utilities to the same extent as the great system of hydroelectricity in Ontario of which this province is so proud and which, I would remind the Conservative party, was established by a great Canadian, Sir Adam Beck. But perhaps the Conservative party may have changed since it added the word "Progressive" to its name, though it is, in any case, a strange combination of names. Yes, the Ontario hydroelectric system of which the people of that province are so proud was promoted by Sir Adam Beck but built by a Conservative government of that province.
It may be said by somebody, in connection with all this, that there may very well be some Canadian control over these companies. I notice that the Minister of Public Works dealt with that matter in the House of Commons during the debate in 1956. On page 2195 of Hansard he discounted a statement

made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce very well indeed. On March 15, 1956, he said:
The minister has said that shares are to be offered to the Canadian public. He might have gone on to point out that even though several thousand individual Canadian shareholders bought up to 51 per cent of the shares, which is most unlikely-
Of course it has not happened.
-there would be no possible chance that they could overrule these three great United States companies-The Delhi Company is also a United States company-working together as a closely knit unit. It is absolutely fantastic to suggest that private Canadian shareholders would have the slightest chance of controlling the company. Control rests with these United States companies and it is going to remain there unless the government makes some change in its policy.
I say those words are as true today as they were in March, 1956. What steps will the Conservative government of Canada, which so bitterly opposed this bill when in opposition, take to ensure to the people of Canada the public use, public control and public profit with regard to these utilities which the people of Canada have financed already, in part, and which they will finance to an even greater extent when the pipe line goes forward. It is not yet built. We have an opportunity now. I challenge the government to seize that opportunity and to do the right thing in this regard.
Having said this, I want to put on record again the amendment I moved to the speech from the throne, because now, I think, it may be better understood than when I introduced it on Wednesday afternoon, wishing to make sure that the amendment would be introduced that day:
This house welcomes the measures indicated in the speech from the throne and urges that these measures be placed before parliament with the least possible delay in order that the benefits proposed therein might accrue to the Canadian people at once. We respectfully submit, however, that in the opinion of this house Your Majesty's advisers should give immediate consideration to the advisability of taking steps to deal with the menace of inflation, rapidly rising unemployment and other serious problems facing this country. We call upon the government to give immediate effect to the social and economic planning necessary to cope with these problems.
As clearly as I am able, I have pointed out to the government what in my opinion is its duty in this regard. I wish to reiterate, before I sit down, that we welcome the measures announced in the speech from the throne, measures which we-though not we alone-have long advocated, namely an increase in the pensions provided for our senior citizens, an increase in disability pensions, an increase in pensions for the blind, an increase in pensions for our war veterans, some steps toward a stabilization of agricultural prices to prevent a continuance of

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to make a short statement on my position as member of parliament for the Yukon Territory.
Shortly after the result of the general election had been announced my Conservative opponent challenged the legality of the election on the grounds that there were irregularities in the taking of the vote. The charge was heard before two judges, as provided for in the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. Last week they gave their decision, to the effect that irregularities had taken place in the taking of the vote and that the election should be voided.
I should add, Mr. Speaker, that the judges found no evidence of fraud or corruption, but merely of minor technical irregularities committed by the supporters of both candidates. I am afraid that our ways in the Yukon are more casual than in the more densely populated areas of Canada, and we have generally been more concerned with the spirit rather than the letter of the law. An election act designed for taking the vote in southern Canada is not necessarily the best way to get out the vote in the vast reaches of the Yukon Territory. Because of our sparse population, everyone knows everyone else, and so the special identification requirements of residents not on the voters lists are scarcely needed in the Yukon. Therefore I would respectfully suggest that the elections act be amended to remedy these special problems peculiar to the northland.
Perhaps the house would be interested in the type of irregularities discovered. For example, a clergyman resident in Whitehorse preached in Mayo Landing, a settlement 250 miles north of Whitehorse, the Sunday before the election and cast his vote there, as he would not be back in Whitehorse until after election day. Another clergyman of a different faith cast his vote at the proper poll, but the poll was a divided one and the ballot was put in the wrong box. There were many

The Address-Mr. Low others in the same position as the clergyman I have just mentioned who were absent from their normal places of residence, but who voted at polls in the communities they happened to be in on June 10.
Disfranchisement of our citizens in my opinion is not the intention of the act. Every Canadian no matter where he lives in Canada should be given every opportunity to exercise his franchise. When such errors could be made in good faith by clergymen, it is easy to understand why other minor technical errors were made by other persons.
I have the right to appeal the decision of the judges to the Supreme Court of Canada, and to hold my seat until their decision is reached. I have decided, however, not to exercise this right but to accept the judgment of the lower court and vacate my seat when the court order is formally received by Mr. Speaker.
I do this, Mr. Speaker, in order that there may be no cloud on the Yukon representation. Our great territory needs an active spokesman in parliament and I urge the government to call the by-election as soon as possible so that a Yukon member can be seated without undue delay. The constituents of this important, far-flung riding expect the government to take prompt action to avoid further resentment and annoyance, and to give them the representation they so justly deserve in this House of Commons.
I believe it is possible to call the election before Christmas, which would permit representation in parliament in January. As a man who has lived almost all his life in the Yukon I can assure this house, Mr. Speaker, that it is perfectly possible to have a winter election there, because we have certainly solved the problems of transportation and communications in winter. All the remote settlements not served by highway are readily accessible by ski-equipped aircraft.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be proper for me at this time to speak on any of the many Yukon problems which need attention. I shall reserve those remarks until I return from winning the by-election, which I hope will be called for December.

Not only that but unfortunately a good many of the things that have been said by them in the past are now being thrown into their faces. I suppose this goes to show that we all have to expect these chickens to come home to roost, and I would imagine that if by some ill wind that should chance to blow my hon. friend across the way ever formed the government of Canada, a lot of these things which have been said by him and members of his group in the past would be thrown back at them with equal vehemence and equal effect.
I must say, though, that the government is in the enviable position of having people pay great tributes to it, and I can only say that never in my experience have so many opposition parties and members been determined to keep a government in office. This is indeed an unusual circumstance. All governments that I have seen thus far are ones that the opposition wanted to defeat at the first opportunity, but here we have a changed circumstance and what a drastic change it is. I am sure the people of the country will watch with vast interest what happens here in the next few weeks.

supreme politicians from the statesmen in parliament, and it will be most interesting to see into what category various hon. members fall.

Well, it is something to be a part of the dog which is something I am afraid my hon. friend cannot say.
I would like to turn, sir, for a while now to a discussion of the provisions of Her Majesty's speech. We were glad to see that the government is prepared to fulfil its election promises in connection with old age pensions, war veterans allowances, pensions for the blind and pensions for the disabled. These are things which we have fought for constantly over the years. Reference to these matters in the speech from the throne was in very general terms, as has already been 

pointed out. Nothing definite is yet known about the amount of the increases or when the increases will be made effective. I presume that in good time the government will make these things known to us and that at that time we shall be in a far better position to express our views about them. However, I should like to say that the government is to be commended on thinking about our aged citizens, the veterans and the unfortunate ones in our country. Surely, it must have been evident to any thinking person that our senior citizens should not be expected to try to eke out a miserable existence on $46 a month, in the light of the serious increases, as it were, being made almost monthly in the cost of living.
We think that long ago there should have been an escalator provision in the old age and blind pension arrangements, and perhaps even in the war veterans allowance arrangements, to make possible automatic increases to take care of increases in the cost of living. We are impressed by the fact that the government recognizes the need for increases and that they are prepared to make some provision for them. We want them to know that we support also any effort that will be made to shorten the residence qualifications and we believe that since old age pensions are now contributory they should be paid as of right to the recipient no matter where he may live. We ask the government to take that matter into very serious consideration.
I am certain that the people of Canada generally are aware of the fact that if the Conservative government can increase old age and blind pensions and war veterans allowances in October of this year there is no reason whatsoever why the Liberal government could not have done an equally good job in March of the same year or even earlier. In the intervening months so far as I know there has been no real change in the economic condition of the country, certainly no upsurge or change for the better which would justify the Liberals in saying that they could not do it.
There is one thing however, that the government must bear in mind and that is this. Unless something fundamentally sound is done to check the continuous price rise, what they have proposed to help the aged, the blind and the war veterans will be of no lasting value whatever. One of the big reasons why the people of Canada elected a new government last June was that they wanted people in office who would bring to bear upon the problems of the country a different approach and different thinking, and especially people with the mental attitude that says, "it can be done."

It is refreshing, therefore, to see the new government taking the stand in some things that changes for the better can be made, and for that I congratulate them. I suggest it is time that a new approach was made to financial policy because I am convinced that with a fresh attitude towards it something of a worth-while nature can be accomplished that will be of lasting advantage, not only to the aged, the infirm and the disabled but to all the people of Canada. I hope that the Conservative government will not get into the same frame of mind that was so obvious all the while the Liberals were in office. From 1935 to 1957 they seemed to feel that so far as financial policy was concerned the present state of affairs was the necessary state of affairs. They constantly indicated the closed mind on that subject and the people of the country just got tired of it. Therefore I throw out the warning to the government that they will have to be very careful not to fall into the same frame of mind as did the Liberal government, especially with respect to this most important fundamental, a sound monetary policy. It is easy to do that, especially when ministers of the crown depend so much for their advice on the civil servants they inherit. That does not cast any reflection whatsoever on the civil service of Canada.
I sincerely hope that the old age pensions, blind pensions, war veterans alowances and disability pensions are given a substantial boost at this time, one that will be in keeping with the needs of the good people concerned as well as with the productive capacity of this great country. I suggest that a $60 a month basic pension for the aged would not be out of line at all.
We noted with some satisfaction that the government is to provide cash advances to farmers against farm-stored grain. We have already made our position clear in this regard in previous debates of other years. We think that cash advances are more fair than and preferable to government guaranteed loans through the chartered banks. Here again, Mr. Speaker, the details of the government's proposals have not been revealed to us and we will have to wait until we see exactly what the program is before we can go too much into detail in our discussion. We sincerely hope, however, that this is not the sum total of the government's program for assuring the farmer his fair share of the national income.
Her Majesty's speech does indicate in a rather indefinite way that parliament will be asked to enact a measure to provide greater stability in the prices of farm products. These words may refer to the commodity price support legislation now on the
The Address-Mr. Low statute books of the country but which was never put into effect fully by the former government. It must be clear to the present government that some definite provision will have to be made through stabilization of prices and marketing arrangements, and perhaps in other ways, to assure the farmer his fair share of the national income.
My colleagues and I have been advocating various measures for years which we thought would have to be applied if the aggregate income of Canadian farmers was to bear a fair relationship to farm costs. It will not be good enough in my judgment to provide cash advances against farm-stored grain and that only. At best these cash advances can only make available to the farmers a small amount of cash to meet their most pressing bills and keep them one step ahead of the sheriff. Moreover, the government is going to find tremendous difficulties in taking security and in making the advances.
The situation would be far different if the former government had been wise enough to provide approved storage as they should have done. I do not mean to imply that the farmers of this or any other country have to be molly-coddled or want to be because I am sure they do not want to be, but I think it can be laid down as a sound principle that governments should do for the people those things which they cannot do for themselves or things that the government can do so much better. Provision of adequate inland and terminal storage facilities for grains especially is one of these things that enlightened, forward-looking governments have felt it their duty to provide. In the United States the government has doubled the amount of storage capacity for farm products since 1953, and thus when surpluses mounted approved storage was available and that made it much simpler to make cash advances against farm products properly stored.
I think that this government must face up to the fact that in the years ahead it will be desirable in the interests of our national security and in the interests of the hungry people of the world for Canada to have enough inland and terminal storage capacity properly and wisely dispersed to carry over safely from one year to another not less than two full years' grain production. When the time is more appropriate I intend to put forward to the house an irrefutable case for the establishment of a 2 million bushel storage elevator in the Peace river country, my own constituency, as one unit in what will be a necessary, broader government program. Here again the people of Canada are bound to ask if the Conservative government can make available cash advances to the farmers in the

The Address-Mr. Low fall of 1957, why could not the Liberals have done equally well in the spring of 1957 or 1956 or 1955 or even earlier?
However that may be, the problems facing the farmer will not be solved unless and until great improvements have been made in marketing and in pricing. We are convinced that the basis of any real improvement in the farmers' position will be the adoption of the two-price system that has been used so successfully by many industries in this country. Colleagues of mine will go more fully into this situation in the course of their speeches.
I note some rather vague references to taxation in the speech from the throne. I sincerely hope that this is not merely window dressing in preparation for another election. The people of Canada are expecting relief from the heavy burden of taxation. One of the reasons they changed governments was the failure of the Liberals to come to grips seriously with the whole taxation problem. I think the former minister of finance must have realized that when he took upon himself this summer much of the burden for the loss of government status by the Liberals. The government will have to realize that what I am saying is true and if they ever expect seriously to tackle the increasing cost of living they will have to begin to remove those taxes that inevitably push up prices and add to the burden of consumer costs.
One of the most prolific causes of inflation is the government's habit of imposing hidden taxes against commodities, and a right good place to start tackling the cost of living problem and the rise of the price index in any program of tax reduction is in the field of commodity taxes, the sales and excise taxes that are applied at the manufacturers' level.
Of course, the Canadian people would welcome a reduction in income taxes. I am told that if some relief in income taxes is provided Canadians generally are prepared for the time being to forget all the others so that they can at least sleep nights.
The government is to be commended for their intention to propose from time to time projects and programs to implement a national development policy which is to be carried out in co-operation with the provinces and territories and which will enable all regions of Canada to share in the benefits to be realized from the development of the resources of this great nation. But I warn the government that as they proceed to develop the ideas programs and projects for this purpose they will come face to face inevitably with the absolute necessity for a change in the financial policy of this country. I point out that financial policy and national


development are inevitably and unalterably tied together. If the government is to fulfil its promise to give effect to proper national development policies they will have to change their whole approach to finances in Canada, particularly their concept of the role and functions of the Bank of Canada. They will not get far if they do not solve the tight money problem and come to a definite decision with regard to this very important question. Who is to devise and lay down financial policy in this country? Is it to be a bunch of jobbers or must it be the parliament of this land?
I think one of the most serious omissions in the speech from the throne is the lack of any mention whatever of the tight money policy of the previous government. Thus far I have seen little evidence that the new government is prepared to come to serious grips with this disastrous policy. They must know-I am speaking now of this government-as many thinking people across this country are coming to know that the tight money policy of the Liberal government was a policy laid down largely by the Bank of Canada. It is a policy which was enunciated about two years ago and was supposed to have accomplished three things. According to the governor of the Bank of Canada, it was designed to bring about a reduction in the cost of living or at least to curb rising consumer costs. In the second place, it was supposed to bring about a reduction in Canada's serious adverse balance of trade. Thirdly, Mr. Coyne's policy was supposed to bring about a reduction of the huge consumer debt that had been brought about very largely by credit buying.
Those are the three things that the governor of the Bank of Canada and his associates emphasized and about which they expressed deep concern in the banking and commerce committee in 1955. I ask hon. members of this house to pause for just one moment and think of what has happened since then. The government of Canada established a market for treasury bills, that was the Liberal government, and they allowed the interest rate on those to rise to 4 per cent. Following this the Bank of Canada claimed that they had no alternative but to increase the rediscount rate to 4 per cent. The governor of the Bank of Canada issued requests at the same time, which many people of course interpreted as commands, to the chartered banks of this country to restrict credit. This they immediately started to do. As a consequence the tight money policy was foisted upon the people of Canada. General interest rates jumped by more than 1 per cent in a single

year; development in many areas of Canada fell off seriously and soon came to almost a full stop in several areas. Our municipalities, school divisions and provincial governments were forced to either completely curtail their present projects or go into the money markets of the United States to borrow to fill their money needs.
The tight money policy which started in 1955 has unquestionably been a miserable failure. Let us take a look at what has definitely happened in those two years in the three important things Mr. Coyne's policy was supposed to have accomplished. I remind you that it was supposed, in the first place, to curb the rising cost of living. Has it done so? Well, in September 1956 the consumer price index stood at 119, and today it stands at 122.6, the highest in history, and it continues to go up. Unless something is done about it, Mr. Speaker, I predict that within a year it will stand at 125. The fact is Mr. Coyne's policy, rather than curbing living costs, has actually built into our economy definite inflationary trends, some of them on a long-term basis.
Consider for example, if you will, the serious increase in mortgage interest rates. The family man who tries to provide a home today finds that as a result of the credit restrictions and tight money policy he must contract to pay higher interest rates, not just for one year but over a period of 15 or 20 years, no matter how interest rates may go down in the next few years. That is what I call built-in inflation over a long period of time. What strikes many people as very odd about this whole situation is that prices go on rising in spite of the fact that industrial and business inventories have been accumulating at a rapid rate over the last two years. There have been very few commodities in short supply, except money and the will in high places where policy is made to tackle the problem in such a way as to help the average citizen. Mr. Coyne's policy has been a miserable failure too, so far as reducing the cost of living is concerned or even in curbing the rising cost of living index.
What about the second thing Mr. Coyne's policy was supposed to have accomplished, namely a reduction in our adverse balance of trade? Since the tight money policy began in 1955 our adverse balance has more than doubled, and so the tight money policy has been a miserable failure in this branch also.
What about the third reason for Mr. Coyne's policy? How has it operated in connection with consumer debt since 1955? The governor of the Bank of Canada expressed grave concern two years ago over the tremendous increase in credit buying by Canadian people.
The Address-Mr. Low If I remember my figures correctly, in 1955 consumer debt brought on by credit buying by the people of Canada stood at about $2.2 billion. Today it stands at no less than $2.6 billion which is a good $400 million above the figure for 1955. This simply means, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada have had to mortgage future incomes to the extent of $2.6 billions in order to satisfy present needs and wants out of the great pile of production already in existence and crying for a market. I say that nothing emphasizes quite so much as this fact the imperative need for a new approach to our whole financial policy in Canada.
We Social Crediters have that approach. Our financial policy can solve this problem and can make completely unnecessary the tight money policy. It must be evident to hon. members of this house that Mr. Coyne's policy has failed all the way along the line. In fact it has intensified inflationary trends rather than reduced them. I remember back in 1955 that one of the reasons given by Mr. Coyne for initiating the policy of credit restriction was a claim of insufficiency of labour in Canada. I think it can be safely said that the framers of the policy cannot use that argument now, because the dominion bureau of statistics reports that today the registered unemployed labour force stands at 174,000 individuals, and it is growing daily.
We are charging Mr. Coyne with foisting upon Canada a policy of foolish restrictions just at a time when our chief competitor, Russia, is going all out to expand all the way along the line. This in our judgment puts us in a very dangerous position. I bring these things to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because this government will have to face up to the situation in a very realistic manner. They will have to make it abundantly clear to the Bank of Canada that financial policy from this time forward is going to be framed by the parliament of Canada. Until the government makes that point very clear and then sets about asking parliament to give Canada a new, realistic financial policy, they never will be able to fulfil their campaign promises. In fact the best thing we will be able to do will be to take care of the fringe things, that is until they fight out this battle with the Bank of Canada and win.
We commend to the government a serious and uninhibited study of Social Credit financial proposals. I am sure they will find in them the real foundation for the establishment in Canada of a policy of freedom. Moreover, they will find in the techniques we suggest for the application of that policy the only hope in the world today for individual liberty. We see most of the present

The Address-Mr. Low policies stripping the individual of his liberties and progressively narrowing his range of free decisions.

The Address-Mr. J. B. Hamilton man in the street, the little man who saw things happening which could not be seen by those who were engrossed in the study of their own balance sheets.

As a matter of fact there was the same breakdown in the lines of communication with our neighbour to the south, a breakdown that left us with no say in procedures of investigation affecting the rights and political status of our own citizens. The general deterioration of our international trading position, the continuing pile-up of our western wheat crops, the mounting trade deficit on current account and the situation in which more and more of our basic industries are owned outside our own country were also among the realities which were not being faced.

No one wants an economic benefit while others suffer, but I am wondering whether we have not reached the point where if we are to maintain control of our own resources, have the wherewithal to do it, we may not have to say to our allies that we must take care of our own economic requirements while they take care, on a larger scale, of continental defence. Mr. Speaker, it is with a legitimate pride that I rise today in the house. After having been away for three years, I am glad to be back in the house where I am pleased to see again many a familiar and friendly face, and where I also find that unfortunately, some of the people I had known have disappeared, swept away, as it were, by the fortunes of politics.
When, in June 1954, I introduced in this house for the last time the estimates of the Department of Transport, I was convinced it would be my last appearance here. After three years as chairman of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, I am glad to be back in politics, and if I have come back to them, it is primarily because I was asked to do so by the right hon. the former prime minister. I could not possibly refuse to co-operate with the leader of the party, who himself had given such an example of sacrifice for the sake of his country by leaving not only his profession, but his family life, in order to dedicate himself to the service of Canada.
In view of this example of devotion to public affairs given to all of us by our leader, I was happy to come back to Ottawa and to find myself again at the side of former colleagues in the House of Commons.
When I quit politics in 1954 to accept the chairmanship of the St. Lawrence Seaway Administration, I was conscious then of doing what I considered to be my duty for the common good of the country. When I returned to active politics, at the side of those with whom I had been associated for some 19 years, I was also conscious of answering a no less urgent call, but in a wider and greater field. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I have no regrets at all about the decision I made because, one way or the other, I felt I was doing my duty.
Speaking in this house for the first time since my return, I am happy to do so in French, as a citizen of a country which is officially bilingual and as a member representing a French-speaking constituency of the province of Quebec. In so doing, I am

conscious of exercising a fundamental right which the Liberal party has always been mindful to respect fully. In the minds of the French-speaking members particularly, that right, which was won following the struggles of the first year of responsible government, constitutes a duty from which they could not shrink without betraying the mandate entrusted to them.

A day or two after the announcement which he made the Vancouver Sun of September 9 had this to say about his decision:
Mr. St. Laurent gained wide respect and admiration for his leadership in international affairs, particularly for his role as one of the fathers of NATO. He certainly was always keenly aware of the big problems of our age and intent upon grappling with them. But his greatest contribution as prime minister of Canada was to Canada, to Canadianism. He reconciled French and English Canada during the war. He was the chief negotiator for Newfoundland's entry into conferedation. His government abolished appeals to the privy council. He appointed the first Canadian governor general.
Of much greater importance, however, was his concept of unity. His message was simple: What French and English have in common as Canadians is far more than the differences that divide them, for it is Canada itself. And this man, straddling the nation's basic split by his very birth, carried the message as few men could.
This is an excellent account of the important part played by our beloved leader. We on this side of the house, as well as all true Canadians will always be most grateful to him for the role and the part which he has played and for the services which he has rendered to Canada in that respect.
Under his able leadership national unity has made great strides. The two main ethnic groups have come to understand each other better and, what is even more important, they have come to undertake national projects, they have come to work hand in hand together with one common end in view, greater Canadian advancement. They have


learned too that after world peace there is nothing more important for this country of ours than national unity, that it is the indispensable basis of all progress in all spheres of our national life.
Unfortunately this national unity which we have acquired in recent years under the leadership of the Liberal party is now being threatened by the political strategy of the Conservative party. I should like to recall some of the history of the Conservative party in that respect before referring to this strategy in detail.
In order to understand the background of the matter, however, we have to remember that Canadians have always been divided into three groups insofar as national unity is concerned. At one extreme there are those Canadians who throughout our history have always been more British than the British themselves, have always been imperialistic in their tendencies and have always thought that it was impossible for French speaking Canadians to be British without ceasing to be French.
At the other extreme, however, there are those Canadians in Quebec who have always been anti-British, who are always reluctant to participate in national undertakings except on their own terms. In fact they think and behave as if Quebec was not an essential part of Canada but a separate state. In the 19th century these people were called the ultramontanes or "Les Castors".
Finally, midway between these two extremes was the great number of Canadians, both English and French speaking, who always had a Canadian outlook, which is certainly not incompatible with a deep attachment to British and French traditions, who accepted quite willingly the fact of our different ethnic origins and who were ready to participate in common undertakings in a spirit of conciliation and mutual respect.
Under the leadership of Macdonald and Cartier the Conservative party was a national party in the true sense of the word. However, quite early in its history, and especially under the leadership of Blake and Laurier, the Liberal party adopted a Canadian outlook and recruited its supporters from the third group of Canadians which I have just described. Since the Liberals occupied the position at the centre, the Conservative party felt itself obliged to seek its support at the extremes among the so-called imperialist group in English speaking Canada and, especially after Cartier's death, among the ultramontane group in Quebec.
Since these two extreme groups had nothing in common with each other there was only

one alternative for the Conservative party to adopt and it was this, to have two policies, one for Quebec and one for the rest of Canada.

(Peel): Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who has just spoken was not here when the rules were amended so as to impose a definite time limit on speeches in this debate, since when courtesy has required that no one member should exceed the 40-minute period allotted to him in order that every one might have the opportunity to express their views.
I would also add, Mr. Speaker, that the maiden participation of the hon. member for Laurier when he came to the house in 1935 was much more effective than his maiden speech as a private member on the opposition side, because in that participation he made no comments whatever.
As to his remarks in French, they were a little better than his comments in English. He was kind in his comments in French, and it seems to me that when he referred to the

former prime minister he expressed thoughts that we all share. We regret, however, that when that right hon. gentleman was prime minister he saw fit to surround himself with people who did not have quite the democratic tradition that he has, and we regret that those hon. gentlemen still surround him.
As for the little comment which the hon. member for Laurier made in French that during the election never were so many promises made by so few to so many, I suggest to him that never have so few come so far so fast.

speechtext:
Twenty-two years is a long time.
Mr. Pallet!: I am very pleased to have the privilege, Mr. Speaker, of taking part in the debate on a historic occasion such as this. This is a very rare privilege. History was made when a ruling monarch opened parliament. There is no division in this country. All one had to see were people of both tongues turning from that monarch with a smile and a light in their eyes. To think that the hon. member for Laurier would suggest that there was a division-such poorness, such lowness, and many of us thought it did not quite fit in with the person who used once to be-I am sorry the hon. member for Laurier is leaving, because I am not finished with him yet-does not become the occasion.
Perhaps, of course, his general remarks can be taken as being on the same basis of accuracy as those in which he congratulated the mover and the seconder of the address when he said that he shared the same experience on his first visit to the house. I took the liberty while he was speaking of checking Hansard and found his name did not appear in Hansard as either the mover or the seconder of the address. Maybe we should give the same attention to the rest of his remarks as is indicated by the index to Hansard with regard to that particular comment.
I would like to join with others who have spoken in congratulating the Speaker on his elevation to that office. We have known him well, and we have admired him, and I am sure he will discharge his duties with alacrity and fairness. To the Deputy Speaker I wish to say exactly the same thing, and as for the mover and seconder of the address, they spoke with vigour, they spoke with intelligence and they spoke with a deep knowledge of the matters that they discussed, a combination which speaks well for this parliament and which augurs well for the future of this country.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) concluded his comments the other day I rather expected that all those
The Address-Mr. Pallett people sitting behind him would get up and cross the floor and attempt to sit on this side of the house. Some of them might have to get used to sitting on the back benches here, though they had sat on the front benches before. But if the hon. gentleman is correct when he says he represents over half the popular vote of the country, is he being fair in not giving those people whom he represents an opportunity to express their views in the expected fashion?
If, on the other hand, the view of the members of the constituencies which his party represents are the same as the views of members on this side of the house, does he not think they should be given an opportunity to express those views, and soon?
It should be comforting to hon. members on this side to note that there have been other occasions when an amendment was not moved on the address, and they were usually followed in the ensuing election by a thundering defeat of the party which failed to move it.
On the subject of criticism: The Leader of the Opposition says he is not going to criticize; his party are going to make minuscule suggestions, but they are not meant to be taken seriously. He has placed an extra burden on hon. members on this side, but one which I am sure they will discharge with a full sense of their responsibility, a sense of responsibility which was completely missing on the government side in the last parliament.
We are quite prepared to perform a double function on this side; the government will introduce legislation and hon. members sitting beside and behind the government are quite prepared to criticize that legislation so that when it leaves this house it will be in a form as perfect as their efforts can make it. This was a matter in which, during the last parliament, hon. members then supporting the government failed in their responsibility, but I can assure the people who now make up the government that their own members will watch their legislation.
Do not be surprised if we criticize it because that is our function in this house. I also assure them, Mr. Speaker, through you, that knowing the lady and gentlemen who make up the government we have the utmost confidence that the legislation they introduce will be, not only sound, fair and well drafted but by and large will represent the views of the country as a whole.
The events of June 10 raised the horizons and opened new vistas for Canada. Canadians can now go forward in solid step, surmounting the supineness of the last 22 years. The step

The Address-Mr. Pallett will be quickened. It will be to good purpose if we follow a course of high principle and dedication and not one of expediency.
On the debate on the address it is customary to deal with some matters concerning one's own riding. I do so with no diffidence whatever because the county of Peel is one that owes a great deal to this country. We feel we are rather fortunate in that we have every means of transportation including road, rail, airport and deep sea water. We have ideal agriculture and the best industrial sites in Canada. Ours is a fast-growing, rapidly developing section of this country. A great many of the problems we meet, I think, are not unlike the problems that are met by the rest of the country and certainly our agricultural and horticultural problems are much the same.
We are pleased that the government has taken some steps to assist the agricultural industry. We anticipate that more steps will follow and that the agriculturists and horti-culturalists will be enabled to receive their fair share of the national income.
I come next to aircraft production. In Peel county we have a large industry centring around the production of aircraft and employing many thousands of workers. It has been in the forefront of aeronautical activity for years. The workers in those plants cannot be allowed to be subject to the whims and vagaries of defence requirements as they exist from day to day. These workers are highly trained and skilled and constitute a valuable pool. It is up to the private industry in which they work and other groups to ensure that their employment is guaranteed. The future of Canada is in the air and we in Peel are fortunate that we can make such a marked contribution to that future.
The next matter with which I choose to deal is housing. Although we welcomed the announcement of the release of $150 million, that in itself is not and will not be sufficient. Our municipalities want housing developments and we are aware that such developments create employment. There is no industry in the county that of itself creates as many jobs as does housebuilding. We also know that in the development of subdivisions many problems arise. We cannot have new homeowners paying extra levies to take care of capital construction costs of services if we follow the principle of maintaining low-cost housing.
At one time the municipalities were prepared to accept the burden of this cost of providing services but today they cannot do this. I am informed a dominion-provincial conference will be held shortly. We anticipate-and we trust we are right in our 
anticipation-that moneys will be made available to the provinces to pass on to the municipalities to handle the cost of these new services so we as a federal body can provide the necessary low-cost housing and the accompanying employment which it is our responsibility to do.
Previous parliaments have seen fit to increase the funds set out for the elimination of level crossings in this country. Traversed as we in Peel county are by two main lines, both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific railway, there are many level crossings in my riding which present both a problem and a hazard. I am pleased to say it is contemplated that one of the most serious and dangerous of those crossings will be eliminated with construction commencing in 1959. That is a perfect example of co-operation on three levels of government, if I may express it that way, and I welcome the announcement of the elimination of the crossing north of Port Credit on No. 10 highway.
I come now to a subject that has been mentioned on the floor of this house many times, the fate of the Long Branch rifle ranges. Much was said but not too much was done about this. It now appears that it can be said the ranges have been declared surplus and subject to the requirements of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario for the building of its massive generating plant, the lands of the city of Toronto can be dealt with and the balance may be referred to the municipality of Toronto township. That to me was a very welcome announcement. It will require a working out of details but I was pleased to learn that these valuable lands which have been dormant for so long can now once more be made useful.
We in the county of Peel and I am sure all hon. members of this house welcome the social security measures set forth in the speech from the throne. Because of our industry and the generally high level of employment the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) receives what we at least consider to be more than his fair share of the revenue from Peel county. We realize that with increased social services we will perhaps be paying a large portion of the cost of those services for other parts of the country. Nevertheless I say to this house we do not regret this situation in the least because we know that social services wherever they may be not only help the economy, but what is more important they assist those who are not able to help themseelves. The fact that we can participate in this way makes us proud of our present government in that it has seen fit to include mention of this type of legislation in the speech from the throne.

On behalf of my riding I wish to pay personal tribute to our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). The hon. member for Laurier has not yet realized what has happened. There was a spark that lit the fire of democracy in this country. It has nothing to do with the division of the races. You know I have a name that is pronounced differently in Ontario from the way it is pronounced in Quebec. The hon. member for Laurier made a speech. It was different when he represented a riding in Ontario from what it is when he represents a riding in Quebec. This is the first time in this house that I have ever heard him make that type of speech. He made it because he is now from a Quebec riding. Read the speeches he made when he was from an Ontario riding. You will find they were quite different. If he wants a lesson on national unity let him read the speeches of our Prime Minister. There is a man we congratulate as a political winner, a man who knows how to put first things first and a man who has restored the jaunty step to Canadians.
