speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a newly elected member I am pleased to be able to speak in the throne speech debate at this time through the courtesy of my colleagues. I was pleased with the promises implied in the throne speech but at the same time was very disappointed by the fact that the needs of the unemployed in the lumbering industry particularly were overlooked, or worse still, not recognized. The inflation that cuts into everyone's pocket and steals half the pay cheques of our workers creates an emergency situation that is in no way alleviated.
Many of the problems of my constituents are pressing and I must ask for some consideration from the house regarding those problems. As I listened a few moments ago to the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) I wondered whether he is afraid that perhaps his party will be forced to pass the legislation that we have all wanted and waited for for so long and which is only hinted at in the speech from the throne.
I come from a riding that is dependent to a large extent on the gold mining industry, the riding of Timiskaming, and I should like to say a few words on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and its position in my area. I was pleased to be able to read in Hansard of June 12, 1956, at page 4972, a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in which he said:
I have emphasized, sir, that this measure-
The Address-Mr. Peters
He was speaking of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I continue:
-is no solution of the deep-seated problem of the gold mining industry. The difficulty and the flaw in measures of this kind is that they often lull the government and lull parliament into thinking that the problem has been solved, or at least the problem has been met for the time being. No hon. member should delude himself into thinking that this measure is any solution, even on the short-run basis, of the needs and the problems of the gold mining industry. These problems are going to require much more farsighted solutions than are offered by the hand-to-mouth, stop-gap type of assistance that we have in the present measure.
I wish to say that I agree wholeheartedly with his views, and we look forward to hearing something more very soon on the things that he said could be done for these people and these mines that are existing on emergency gold mining assistance, but we look at it from a different point of view. We think that the act did not go far enough. It did not go far enough for the simple reason that it offered no assistance to be made available to the mining communities and the miners in those communities. Some stipulation must be put in the act so that the workers in those communities and the communities themselves will receive some benefit from the assistance.
I believe the Canadian people have been pleased over the years to be able to do something for a situation which was not the making of the mining industry itself. As everyone knows, the price of gold is a set price. It appears to be much too low for the economy of Canada today. The situation has developed where the people of the mining communities have had to exist on wages that are substandard by all accounts, and certainly are not in keeping with the standard of living which is enjoyed by miners in other fields throughout Canada.
We have found that the assistance has been of little value to communities like Matache-wan and Cobalt. Matachewan is an example where cost aid was paid and it did not eliminate the problems of those mines. They eventually shut down. We have found that although the people were willing to subsidize that industry no provision was made for assistance to encourage secondary industries to come into the community so that when the day comes that the mines disappear, when they are no longer advantageous to operate, there would be something for that community to turn to in the form of secondary industry. The people who have gone into the mining communities and established their homes in those communities should be given some consideration, even if it means that the government may find it necessary to subsidize secondary industries, at least in their initial settlement in that area, so that there will be some continuity in those communities and

The Address-Mr. Peters they will not be left in the position that Matachewan, part of Kirkland Lake and a number of other communities find themselves in at the present time.
I think everybody knows the history of Cobalt. We have found that that town has continually suffered from booms and busts. Recently, the previous government had a contract on a long-term basis under which they subsidized the production of cobalt. Cobalt is a strategic metal and I think that even more than gold it should be considered when subsidies are paid. We have been subsidizing cobalt, as I say, but the term basis has disappeared and cobalt is no longer of any account. Cobalt is not even being developed. If it should become necessary to procure cobalt, in the event of an emergency, development work is not being done. In these mining communities they have not blocked out the amount of cobalt ore that remains in the mines. As a miner of many long years experience underground I know that the people in those mining communities must be given assistance, not only so that dividends can be paid but so that decent wages can be paid and working conditions can be improved in those mines. Consideration should be given to the communities in which the miners live.
In my particular area there is a large iron ore development. This development is taking place in a community called Dane. It requires some assistance to get it started. A large company has come in and bought up the rights. The ore is there. We have the miners available in the area but so far nothing has been done. We would suggest that the federal government give some consideration to subsidizing freight rates in that area in order to get this mine into production as soon as possible.
One of our primary industries in Timis-kaming is lumbering. If there is a field that has been neglected in the speech from the throne that we are now asked to consider it is, I am sure, the lumbering industry. The white pine industry is faced this year with a situation where all its lumber is in the yards in Temagami and Matachewan. Throughout the White River area no lumber has been sold this year and very little was sold last year. This problem rests directly on the doorstep of the government and its tight money program.
In speeches that have been made we have heard references to the sum of $150 million for housing. It would appear to me that the $150 million is not going to be of much more benefit than the money available before because the working people are not able to buy or build houses on account of the great

difficulty they have in obtaining the down payment. I would suggest that we should consider some of the plans that have been followed in the last few years and in the last few months, particularly at Blind River, Elliott Lake and Bancroft. At these places other methods have had to be used than those found under the National Housing Act to promote housing in those areas. I certainly hope that the government will consider extending the application of the methods used at these places with respect to down payments so that we can get the housing industry started again and get our lumber moving from northern Ontario.
I suggest that no solution for the sale of our lumber can be found by asking the producers to reduce the price because I do not think we will even then find any market for it. We are again faced with the problem of imports in the form of very fine plywood. By "fine" I do not mean that it is exceptionally good plywood; it is very thin plywood. In fact, we do not cut veneers that thin. This plywood is coming into Canada, and I suggest we are going to have to do something to expand our markets in the lumbering field so that we can market our products from east to west rather than from west to east as we are now doing.
In Timiskaming we have probably one of the finest agricultural areas in Ontario. We find in that area, as I think is true in many other areas, a great number of farmers leaving the farms. There is one particular township near my home in which at one time there were over 100 farmers and that area is now supporting only five full-time farmers. If the situation has not reached the catastrophic stage, in my opinion it has pretty nearly done so.
I should like to suggest that I believe the throne speech should have included something with regard to parity prices for farm products based on the cost of production of the product compared with the selling price that the farmer receives, parity being the amount of profit that the farmer could reasonably expect should be maintained.
We find farmers in Timiskaming growing some of the finest timothy seed that has been produced anywhere in Canada. During the recent election campaign the government's candidate suggested that if elected he would be able to find international markets for timothy seed. If such markets for timothy seed do exist then I ask the government to take advantage of them without delay so that some of our farmers who are finding it exceedingly difficult to exist at the present time will have a good cash crop.

Yesterday we heard something about rain and drought and have read about these things in Hansard in past years. In northern Ontario we are not particularly worried about drought but we are worried about rain and unseasonable weather. Our growing season is short and on many occasions we find ourselves not able to get our crops into the barns with the results that there is very little money for the family on the farm with which to live throughout the year. I suggest that some consideration be given by the Department of Agriculture to encouraging the provinces to set up crop insurance and, if it can be set up, help to finance such a scheme.
We also suggest that this could be extended to take care of crop failures so that something will be available to alleviate such situations. I should like to point out that last year the grain in the fields was not good on most of the farms in the clay belt of Timis-kaming. When the farmers went to get seed grain in the spring they found they had to borrow money from the banks to buy it and that the price was out of their reach. The result was that inferior grain was planted, grain with a germination of only 15 per cent in some cases. I believe consideration should be given to alleviating this problem of the farmers in my riding.
I do not want to take too much time but I should like to say that in my riding there is a very large lake, lake Timiskaming. It is 85 miles long and a number of miles wide. On that lake there are a number of steamers. There is a pulp log flow through the lake to south Timiskaming pulp mills. There are a large number of private craft on the lake. At Haileybury the dock is such that it cannot even be used for docking a small boat and the dock at New Liskeard was destroyed by fire. I suggest that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) should give consideration to the restoration of both these docks as they are vitally important to a number of people and are most necessary to the pleasure craft that make use of the lake.
I support the amendment because it will result in the realization of some of the promises made in the throne speech, because it deals with other problems that have not been mentioned that affect my riding and because it requests that immediate consideration be given to some of the larger problems such as national health insurance. Some protection must be afforded in the face of the disaster of rising unemployment, the disaster of low and in some cases negligible farm income and the rapidly rising cost of living. I ask the house to give consideration to these most pressing problems.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted first to congratulate you upon your election as Speaker of the house. We are confident that, as your predecessors, you will do honour to the functions of Speaker by maintaining our parliamentary discussions on a dignified level and by being fair to all members of this distinguished assembly. I am also pleased to say how much I appreciated the form, the elegance and the delivery of the speeches made by the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Smith and Arsenault), even though I confess that I do not agree with everything they have said concerning the government's program for this session.
Mr. Speaker, I feel I must take this occasion of my maiden speech in this house to go back to the last general election held in Canada, in the province of Quebec, and particularly in the fine constituency of Dorchester, since this election will no doubt go down in history as "the surprise election". As a matter of fact, neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives nor any other political group expected the defeat of the Liberal government.
The Canadian population was visibly satisfied with the St. Laurent government. The reverse would have been surprising since, under the Mackenzie King and St. Laurent ^ administrations, our country, in war as in peace, has known a tremendous development and enjoyed its greatest prosperity.
It is for that reason that the St. Laurent government, at two general elections, has gained the greatest majorities of our political history, without resorting to fraudulent electoral means.
How is it then that the St. Laurent government was defeated at the last election? The explanation is simple: the Canadian people seemed so well satisfied with the external and internal policies of its government, led by a great statesman, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, that the Liberal party was perhaps too optimistic, concentrating all its energies on the administration of the country without taking enough care to show, day by day, how efficient it was. I do not hesitate to say that the St. Laurent government was ahead of its time by eliminating from politics numerous things which form together what is called "electoralism".
There are many who claim that the government was so preoccupied with the continuing process of improving legislation and adminis-

The Address-Mr. Landry tration, in the interest of the Canadian people, that it did not give sufficient thought to its own fate. However, in consideration of the moral and material progress for which it deserves full credit, history will grant it a summa cum laude degree of democratic generosity.
In a much more immediate future the Liberal party can expect another reward: its return to power.
After twenty-two years of uninterrupted government, during which so many marvellous realizations were achieved, it is normal that the Liberal party should regroup its forces in opposition. This is in accordance with the history of all the great political parties in the world. But there are already several serious signs indicating that the Liberals' stay in the opposition will be of very short duration; just time enough to brace up in this refreshing atmosphere. Here are some of those signs:
The memory of the Liberals' achievements is vivid in the people's mind. First of all, even if the Conservatives managed to get a few more members elected than did the Liberals, one must remember that the Liberals obtained 200,000 more votes than the Conservatives, and that it is the number of votes which more adequately reveals the popular appeal of the parties.
The general impression seems to be that the Liberals were swept out of power by accident; over-confidence in their victory at a time when, precisely, the Conservative party was labouring more than ever to improve its electoral machinery. In the opposition, the Liberals will not take long to tone down their over-optimism after twenty-two years of uninterrupted power. Not really expecting to get into power, the Conservative party made a great many promises which were so contradictory that the implementation of some would make it impossible to keep the others; but people always remember election promises, and always callously insist on their being carried out.
While denouncing what they called the incompetence and the mistakes of the Liberal system, our Conservative friends have put themselves under the obligation to prove these accusations once they were in power. Now our new ministers admit one after the other, and even publicly, that there are no scandals, no costly errors, and that very few things will be changed in the administration. This is decisive proof that the Conservatives have, let us say, far overreached themselves in order to find the "mote" in the Liberal

party's eye, and to camouflage the "beam" in their own. Canadian voters will not be slow to recognize those who deceive them and those who tell them the truth.
But now, after having been fooled by the glaring campaign of the last election, which had blinded them, the people are already back on their feet, remembering the deeds of the Liberal rule, including the march of Canada to full nationhood, at the head of the middle powers of the world; the building, over years of very difficult international trade, of a prosperity which is the envy of all nations; a national machinery providing for the economical needs of our country for at least another quarter of a century; social security measures shielding the people from want; family allowances, pensions for the old, the veterans, the blind, and the disabled, unemployment insurance, and soon, I hope, health insurance, if the new government agrees to continue this highly social undertaking, so well started by the St. Laurent administration; a substantial and intelligent help to agriculture, for instance, the price support act; careful thinking, thorough research, and happy solutions to educational and intellectual problems at the national level; and finally, a true policy of national unity in accordance with the generous principles that have inspired the whole public life of a very great Canadian: The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.
These achievements and many others, we, Liberals, are here to make them prevail and to demand that they be continued by the present government, as well as to watch for the carrying out of the promises so lavishly made by our opponents, until the chivalrous revenge which we will no doubt obtain at the next election.
And if our friends opposite try to appropriate credit they do not deserve, for instance, if they continue to give the public the impression that the Liberals made an excessive use of patronage whereas they, Conservatives, abolish political favouritism, we will not fail to straighten the record by showing:
1.	That the Liberal administration has made very little use of patronage.
2.	That there is no more patronage to suppress in federal politics, and
3.	That the change of advertising agencies already made by the Diefenbaker administration is a flagrant breach in this policy of nonpatronage so loudly proclaimed by this government which has, so far, so cleverly played on the keyboard of illusions.

A record full of brilliant deeds, such is the record of the Liberals; bold promises and obstruction to the wonderful work of the Liberal government, such is the record so far of the Progressive Conservatives.
On the other hand, the Liberal party is united, while the Conservative party is suffering, and will suffer for a long time, from the disunity which marked the national convention of last fall.
Under those circumstances, it takes a lot of conservative faith to hope that the new government will live long.

speechtext:
It is appropriate, I think, to say a few words about the last federal election in the province of Quebec. It has been said that on June 10 the Quebec vote was a sentimental one. This is not so. If the people of Quebec have been voting for the Liberal government, it is because on the federal scene, for over half a century, the Liberal mind has seemed far broader than the Conservative mind.
True, the fine personality of prime minister St. Laurent was an important factor. But this is due not so much to the fact that Mr. St. Laurent is of French origin through his father, but rather because he possesses an admirable combination of qualities which ideally fit him for leadership in a heterogeneous nation such as Canada.
And it is precisely because of that that, for two general elections, the party led by Mr. St. Laurent has gained the most decisive victories ever recorded throughout our political history, not only in Quebec, but also in English-speaking provinces.
May I also be allowed to recall the loyalty of the province of Quebec to Mr. Mackenzie King, former Liberal prime minister, whose deeply social and humane outlook has had a most salutary influence over Canadian society, in all respects.
The province of Quebec did not vote for sentimental reasons on June 10 last; it voted for reasonable ones. I would be the first to admit that Quebec, from a political point of view, is far from perfect. But please do not say that we voted sentimentally when we know that twice English-speaking Canadians voted with equal enthusiasm for the same liberal leader! We have paid homage not to Mr. St-Laurent's French name but to his true worth.
And I have no hesitation in adding that such an attitude is in keeping with the prin-
The Address-Mr. Landry ciples of true democracy as well as with the needs of Canadian unity and Canadian progress. Quebec need have no regrets concerning its attitude on June 10. And I do hope such will be the case for the country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, at this point I would like to thank the electors of Dorchester who returned me with a good majority in spite of the coalition and alliance of the Progressive-Conservatives and of the Union Nationale who spared nothing to defeat me. In my constituency, as in many others, all opponents spent fabulous sums during the elections, as is the case in every campaign in which the Union Nationale takes part. This party is far richer than any other for reasons of which everybody is perfectly aware. In spite of everything the people of Dorchester have remained faithful to the Liberal party. And thanks to the young people of my constituency who, nearly to the last one of them, considered your humble servant and the Liberal party as the living impersonation of human liberty, I succeeded in overcoming the oppression of dictator or dictators who put all their faith in asphalt, concrete, brick or gravel rather than in the human value of their constituents. In my constituency as in those of Montmagny-L'lslet, Chicoutimi, Lapointe and so many others, the Diefenbaker-Duplessis axis was not successful.
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with local problems, with which I must deal here in order to properly fulfil my duty to my constituents, I wish to express my opinion on a few general questions while proposing to deal at some other time with other problems of the same nature.
It is unfortunate that Canada should not have its own national flag. On several occasions, the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, has said with his usual and remarkable frankness that he certainly would like to see a truly Canadian flag but on the condition that such a flag be a factor of Canadian unity and not a cause of impassioned controversies and disunity. Should the government succeed in getting all to agree on the project of a truly and exclusively Canadian flag, it will have done a great service to our country, Canada.
I could say as much about a national anthem which should be a hymn of national unity heard with the greatest respect from coast to coast.
The government will soon have to choose a successor to the right hon. Vincent Massey as governor general. It is most important that the next representative of Her Majesty

The Address-Mr. Landry the Queen of Canada be a Canadian citizen. Acting otherwise would be going backwards in our constitutional development. Now, if we want Canadians to have a truly Canadian spirit, they must be satisfied that their only country is Canada, and that it is a sovereign state, without any link of political dependence with either England or the United States, nor any other country. In this way, Canada will be on good terms with every other country and Canadians will all be each other's real friend.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Diefenbaker government, which counts many friends among the Quebec Union Nationale party, to see that the scandal of political influence is stopped with regard to the distribution of old age pensions, and pensions to the blind and disabled. These pensions being paid partly by Quebec and partly by Ottawa, the present federal government should use its friendship with the Union Nationale in order to suppress this preposterous discrimination often affecting our senior citizens, as well as the blind and disabled in Quebec when they are not Union Nationale sympathizers.
May I, Mr. Speaker, now plead for the people of my own riding.
The riding of Dorchester, which stretches along the south bank of the St. Lawrence, is surrounded by the counties of Bellechasse, Lotbiniere and Beauce, as well as by the State of Maine. The riding comprises about 35,000 people who derive their main revenue from agriculture, lumbering, and the maple syrup industries.
In the part colloquially called the "lower county", the soil is rather bountiful and our farmers manage to live, in spite of the nearby cities and the lack of stability in farm prices.
In that part which is called the Upper county, the situation is different; one must go there to appreciate the courage and tenacity shown by our farmers in order to make their lands somewhat productive. Those who come to visit me are always surprised to see, in the fields, huge piles of rocks, which our farmers have removed from their soil. This made one of our good farmers say that he had to till his land, not in rocky earth, but actually in earthy rock. It has therefore become an act of heroism for our people to open up new lands or increase their tillage on lands which have become too small for their needs.
There is often much talk about people leaving the land. This applies to our district perhaps more than to anywhere else,


because the land is not very good for agriculture. That is why, in order to prevent our people from leaving their lands, the government must carry on this stabilizing price policy and even, if need be, improve it so as to provide some measure of security to this large group of our population.
During the last federal campaign, our opponents promised they would increase support prices. I hope they will keep their promise. Here is an example: if we consider that the price of pork-support price, I mean, -is now fixed at 23 cents, such price, according to the Quebec farmers' organ, is but the actual cost price established at 23 cents, which means that any slight loss or accident occurring during breeding means a deficit for the farmer.
Of course, the price of pork, on the Quebec market, is now 30 cents, and perhaps 35 cents in some places; but it happens that many people, who are not farmers, take up hog breeding, the result being an over abundance of this product on the Canadian market. There is therefore, as in the past, a constant threat of a sharp decline in price on the hog market. Those who have begun to sell pork when prices were high are now giving up this business whereas our farmers must continue to live on the land and to accumulate repeated deficits. It would therefore be the proper time for the government to set the support price of pork at 28 cents at least, instead of 23 cents in order to stabilize our market and to allow our farmers to live.
The same holds true of poultry, that is of chicken, the price of which is now 23 cents. I am sincerely convinced that the government should set the support price of poultry at 27 cents.
And again, the same is true of eggs, the floor price of which is at present 38 cents instead of 43 cents, as it should be normally. We must not forget that the support price of these must cover the cost to the farmer of candling and grading, which amounts to approximately 5 cents a dozen. This means that the price of eggs falls to 33 cents when the cost price is fixed at 31 cents.
I would also suggest that the government reduce, on behalf of the farmers, the interest rates on agricultural loans. This rate, I fear, should not exceed 3 per cent, whereas it is now over 5J percent.
As a consequence of the conditions just mentioned, it happens that our farmers, with support prices being so low and soil conditions so poor, have to find a living somewhere

1G7
else. That is why many of them go away for four, six or even eight months a year, to bush camps in order to support their families. Many go to Canadian bush camps (about 6,000) but a great many go to the United States.
For some time, the situation of lumbering has been more than alarming for our people.
I am living in anxiety, with the approaching winter months, for hundreds of homes in my county because I know, for having visited many of them, that hardship will be their lot unless the problem is solved very early.
Several large companies have decided not to cut any lumber this year, and some others have reduced their operations by 50 per cent or even more.
Our bush-camp workers are therefore faced with a problem which will cause in my county such hardship as has been unknown since the 30's. This is an urgent problem for hundreds of families in my county, and I urge the government to consider it as such.
There is, I was assured, in the Unemployment Insurance Act, a clause providing for allowances in extremely urgent cases. I do believe that our bush workers, who now find themselves in a very difficult situation, should benefit from that clause of the unemployment insurance act.
That is why I feel that I must make here a few practical suggestions. The former minister of labour had started negotiations with the administration of the State of Maine with a view to creating a system of reciprocity between that state and Canada, for those of our workers who have to earn their living on the American side. It is well known that under the unemployment insurance act, our bush-camp workers who seek jobs in the United States cannot, when they come back, benefit from Unemployment Insurance, because they have not paid their contributions. I was told that several American states had accepted reciprocity with the exception of Maine and a few others. May I suggest to the Canadian government to keep up negotiations with those American states, in order that Canadians may receive the benefits of unemployment insurance when they come back home. They pay taxes in Canada, and even if they work in the United States, it is still in Canada that they spend their money.
May I also suggest to the government to lift restrictions on farmers who have to leave their land to earn some money, for a part of the year, either as bush-workers or otherwise. According to unemployment insurance regulations, as they now stand, bona fide farmers must have left the farm for a certain number of weeks. The officials concerned
The Address-Mr. Landry generally rule that a farmer who has left his farm for over 22 weeks, or more, in some cases, is eligible for unemployment benefits. This gives rise to constant criticism from our farmers. It also adds greatly to the work which must be performed by the officials of our various Unemployment Insurance offices.
I might also suggest that the district office of St. George de Beauce, which serves most of my constituents, be relieved of part of the load it has to carry. To begin with, the devoted officials at this point should be provided with healthier quarters. Their working conditions should be more humane. Does the department know that from January 1956 to December 1956 the amount of unemployment benefits paid out by this office was $1,106,831.80 as against a roughly equal figure, $1,072,890.50 for the period January 1 1957 to May 31 1957, that is for the first five months of this year, as against the twelve months of last year? Does it know that a total of 38,130 cheques have been issued by this same office? And all this has been accomplished by 16 permanent employees, seven more being employed by the national employment service.
I do feel justified, therefore, in asking that the crowded situation at this district office be remedied by the establishment in my constituency of a sub-office which would serve the parishes of Cranborne, Ste. Germaine, Ste. Rose, St. Camille, St. Louis, St. Cyprien, Ste. Justine and Ste. Sabine.
Because of the great distance between the parishes of St. Leon, St. Malachie and Frampton and the district office in Levis, these communities should also be detached from this office and come under the new sub-office which I would like to see the government establish in my constituency.
While facilitating the work of our employees, at the district office, this improvement would save a lot of money to the unemployed who are often obliged to travel to the district office to file their claim.
The maple syrup industry occupies an important place in the economy of my riding. In fact, every spring, hundreds of our farmers draw from our maple trees that delicious sap later made into maple syrup. Unfortunately, for a few years now, that industry has been suffering from a regression which discourages our producers. In fact, while the cost price of a pound of maple syrup is estimated at 21 to 22 cents, our sugar producers seldom get more than 20 cents a pound. Last year, the Dorchester Maple Syrup Producers Association had to be satisfied, for its production of more than a million pounds, with a selling price of 18 cents while the consumer often had to pay 30 cents, 35 cents and even,
168	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Landry in some cases, up to 50 cents a pound. Of greater consequence still is the fact that markets are now very scarce and that many of our producers still have on hand their 1957 production. Could not the government do, as it does for wheat, butter or for New Brunswick potatoes, make available to the maple syrup industry a certain amount which could be spent first to make this marvellous product known throughout our country and also to provide for a support price for maple syrup, thus ensuring the producer that his yearly production will be sold?
In my opinion, the support price for maple syrup could be set at 28 cents a pound and the government could undertake as it does for other products, to buy the surplus, if need be.

Mr. Speaker, I now wish to say a few words in English on behalf of the several hundred people in my riding who do not speak French. The riding of Dorchester, like several others in Canada, comprises the two elements from which our country was formed, and I must say in this house that, to the satisfaction of all, the two groups get along beautifully in an atmosphere of harmony and mutual help. I am happy therefore to mention these English speaking voters and to assure them of my wholehearted devotion in the service of our riding. May I add, Mr. Speaker, that I am proud to represent such a beautiful riding as Dorchester and to be able, in this chamber, to speak on behalf of such an intelligent people.
I would like, on the occasion of my first speech in this house, to say a word about national unity because I am convinced that national unity is the essential condition of the greatness and strength of our country. Although I am an ardent and earnest follower of Laurier, King, Lapointe and St. Laurent, I have nonetheless deep admiration for Sir John A. Macdonald, who was a Conservative and the co-founder of our Canadian confederation. It was Sir John Macdonald who, on February 17, 1890, in reply to Dalton Mac-Carthy, an influential Conservative of that time, had this to say-and I am translating now from the French version of the original text:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other . . . There is no paramount race in this country; there is no conquered race in this country; we are all British subjects and those who are not English are nonetheless British subjects on that account.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the language of justice and truth and it serves the cause of Canadian unity infinitely better than the slogan repeated here and there during the last electoral cam-


paign in a spirit that is very demagogic but not at all Canadian: "We do not need Quebec to form a government."
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that such provocations will no longer slow down the march of Canadian unity.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I wish to conclude my first speech in the house on a note of national unity because I am convinced that national unity is the primary condition of the greatness and strength of our country.
As I just said in English, I am an ardent and staunch follower of Laurier, MacKenzie King, Lapointe and St. Laurent, four great statesmen who particularly concerned themselves with national unity. I have nonetheless great admiration for Sir John A. Macdonald a former Conservative leader and a co-founder of the Canadian confederation with Sir George Etienne Cartier and other illustrious representatives of both great races making up Canada, the English and the French. It was Sir John A. Macdonald who, on February 17th, 1890, replying to Duncan MacCarthy, a very influential Conservative member at the time, said:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other. I believe that there could be no success in such an attempt and it would be a folly and a malicious thing to do, if it were possible. The statement made that Canada was a conquered country was certainly unhappy.
Whether Canada has been conquered or relinquished, we have a constitution whereby all British subjects are equal, having equal rights in matters of language, religion, property and as individuals. There is no paramount race in this country; there is no conquered race in this country; we are all British subjects and those who are not English are none the less British subjects on that account."
That, Mr. Speaker, is the language of justice and truth which serves the cause of Canadian unity so much better than the slogan repeated here and there during the last electoral campaign in a very demagogic but by no means Canadian spirit "There is no need of Quebec to form a government."
I do hope that such provocations from one side or the other will cease delaying the progress of Canadian unity.
In the circles of the St. Laurent government, which know how to direct the minds towards a generous ideal of Canadian unity -an ideal which is neither French nor English but intensely and profoundly Canadian-no such provocative language is heard from the leaders of that party.
More than his predecessors, Mr. St. Laurent has endeavoured to educate our public men with regard to national unity. In his own party he has forged a spirit so generous, so

broad, so Canadian that, even after his departure-which	he has unfortunately
announced for the near future-the Liberal party will remain the champion of national unity in Canada.
That is why I am a Liberal, Mr. Speaker; that is also why I call upon the public, and particularly on our friends opposite, to find out about the true doctrine which inspires Liberal policy in matters of national unity as well as in other matters of Canadian life. To the extent that there will be sincerity of effort, there will be great cause for gratification.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard over the years of attacks of butterflies in the stomach and jittery feelings when a member arises for the first time to address any legislature and particularly this House of Commons. Well, sir, this is the first time in seven sessions I have had the honour and pleasure of addressing Mr. Speaker and I am frank to say I do not feel too badly about it. True, six of these sessions were spent by me in the provincial legislature and the reason for my reticence in addressing the house then was founded on the fact that when a person occupies the position that you do, sir, and is found talking to himself he is looked upon with a large degree of suspicion.
I want to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your elevation to the high position you now occupy as first commoner of this country and Speaker of this House of Commons. It is indeed a position of great honour and responsibility and I feel you will fill it with honour and dignity. I feel it incumbent on myself to assist in this matter by behaving in an ordinary rational manner.
May I congratulate, too, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) for the able manner in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne or, probably more correctly, the causes of summons.
Contrary to the opinion expressed by an hon. member on the opposite side of the house who rather regretted the fact that the proceedings of parliament were televised on opening day I wish to congratulate those persons who were responsible for televising the opening of parliament. Even granting the rights of hon. members of this house to preserve it from the invasion of outsiders, the rights of the Canadian people to see and hear what is going on in this house do have some place in the annals of this country. I believe that radio and television are an extension of the press. While technically 96698-12
The Address-Mr. Irwin members of the press are not in this house I fail to see that television and radio invade the rights of this house any more than the presence of the press reporters. At least radio and television are factual and not expressions of opinion as to the proceedings.
The constituency which I have the honour to represent is a reasonable cross section of the industrial life of this country having within its boundaries a large number of small industries and many large ones. Also, we have extensive fisheries on the Fraser river and much shipping in the same area.
On examining the text of the speech from the throne I am afraid that my constituents are going to deluge me with queries as to the effect of some of the matters mentioned therein because it is a somewhat nebulous document. I feel it could have been a little more precise in giving the people of this country, and those in my constituency in particular, a feeling that the government intended to implement all the delightful promises that were dwelt upon by my opponent in the election on June 10.
The needs of our senior citizens in the light of rising costs are particularly urgent and already some question has arisen as to the implementation of the extent to which old age pensions should be supplemented. Newspaper reports, which are of course notoriously speculative, have given rise to some doubts in this matter and I sincerely hope the government will go the full distance suggested during the election. Specifically it is to be hoped the government will make it its business to see that the regulations under which the means test is applied are ameliorated to a degree that will permit the participation of a greater number of people who have reached the age of 65.
I am quite well aware, as I was told by the Minister of National Health and Welfare a couple of years ago, that the government denies any responsibility for these regulations but the fact remains if the Department of National Health and Welfare is going to insist on either accepting or rejecting regulations that are sought by the provinces then that department is responsible to that extent for those regulations.
The allowable income under the old age pensions regulations is too restrictive. I am quite sure the government will agree that $46 a month is an impossible income upon which to live in most parts of this country and yet the allowable income, unless it has been raised recently, is only $840 a year. I earnestly suggest that the government give this matter close scrutiny with a view to alleviating these conditions.

The Address-Mr. Irwin
The foregoing remarks regarding old age pensions are most emphatically applicable to war veterans allowances and I sincerely hope the government will adequately implement its promise to see that conditions are made easier for these unfortunate people who have given their services to their country and are now unable to care for themselves. I would like the government to consider altering the regulations for the War Veterans Allowance Act to permit those men who served in the first war and who did not get any further than Britain and are therefore classified as not having served in a war area to be included as eligible for war veterans allowances. It must be remembered that a great many of those men who did not leave Britain were held there for the reason that they were over age. Sure, they lied about their age, but they put no strings on where they were going to serve; they were willing to go anywhere, but because age or health prevented their going any further than the British isles the government has thus far taken it upon itself to rule that they are not eligible for assistance under the act. Certainly they lied about their age, but so what? They were interested in the welfare of Canada and they offered their lives in its defence.
Many of these men have reached an advanced age now. I know one old gentleman who is 92 years of age. He served in the first war under the conditions I described and is now in receipt of only $46 a month. He is not eligible for assistance or treatment under the War Veterans Allowance Act and is forced to live on the paltry sum of $46 a month. I regard this situation as desperately unfair.
There is another class of people that should be considered and that is the widows of war veterans' allowance recipients. When a disability pensioner dies and leaves a widow she is eligible for a pension which may be considered reasonable but the widow of a recipient of the war veterans' allowance is eligible only for a widow's pension and thus is in a different classification from the widow of a disability pensioner. It would be well to ask why, because both are the widows of exservicemen and surely there should be no discrimination as to their status.
Another class that has been discriminated against in my opinion is the Imperial veteran. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that when these men or women comply with a reasonable residence qualification,

and I do not regard 20 years as reasonable-they should be eligible to have their pension from Britain raised to the same level as Canadian pensions for the same percentage of disability or they should at least receive their British pensions in Canadian currency at the old par of $4.86.

At the moment there is a post office in my area which was established under conditions which were not altogether favourable for its establishment. It is a rented building and was built specifically for the Post Office Department but it is in an unfortunate position. It is over to the one side of the area in which I have the honour to serve. It is not central. I believe the lease expires in December of this year and therefore it will be necessary to renew the lease. I sincerely hope that the department of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) will regard this building as being inadequate for the needs of my constituents.
My constituents and I look forward to the establishment of a dominion government building in that area which will serve the needs of the 80,000 people who are residents of Burnaby at the present time. I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) will agree with me that Burnaby as a whole has now arrived at the point where it is entitled to a federal building to house all the various departments of government which are necessary in that fast growing area, and I would respectfully request that the Minister of Public Works give that matter his earnest consideration.
I note there is some indication that this government proposes to co-operate with the provinces in the development of natural resources. Nowhere in this country, Mr. Speaker, will this government find greater scope for activities of this kind than in British Columbia, and from no other source will it reap greater reward. The growth of population in British Columbia since 1941 is 23 per cent higher than the next highest province, Quebec, and nearly twice that of the Canadian average for the same period. This puts a terrific strain on provincial health and welfare services; for the equable climate of the southwest corner of the province makes it a mecca for those seeking refuge from the more rigorous parts of the dominion and the opportunities for advancement hold out an inducement to young men and women to establish themselves and their families there, thus accentuating the pressure on our educational system.
What should be of interest to the dominion government, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the development of British Columbia's natural resources is a veritable pot of gold for the dominion government and yet comparatively it has done nothing in past years but milk the prolific British Columbia cow that has been fed and nurtured by British Columbians. The 1940 report by the Rowell-Sirois commission on British Columbia at page 11 says that the population increase in that province has been greater than in any other province

in this dominion and because of that the pressure on the provincial government is terrific. It is even more important to consider that opinion today because the development in the past seven years has been phenomenal.
The commission to inquire into energy resources, so recently appointed by this government, will in all probability hit a snag in Bill No. 3 passed by this house some three years ago when it considers the development of the Saskatchewan dam. This will also be true of the development of the Columbia river. The water rights act and its regulations in British Columbia are recognized as a pattern for that type of legislation throughout the world and this government would do well to study it, look at some of its effects, and then place their faith for a right and proper development of British Columbia water resources in a government that has the interest of the people of British Columbia at heart.
What benefits British Columbia will benefit Canada, and vice versa. This government will find that co-operation will bring results and to that end the Pacific Great Eastern railway should be of special interest. This railway, stretching as it shortly will from Fort St. John and Dawson Creek to rest its head on the shores of Burrard inlet, taps one of the greatest sources of wealth in this country and offers a scenic trip that is unequalled in a country richly endowed with majestic beauty.
The hon. member for Calgary South made mention of a suggestion that the mayors and reeves should be brought into consultation with the dominion government because they could probably contribute to discussions on dominion-provincial relations. In my opinion the most potent contribution they could probably make is that of convincing themselves that they have sufficient trouble on their hands with their creators, the provinces, without taking on another creation of the provinces, the dominion government.
If the provinces make it their business to maintain their autonomy they will be doing something worth while. This autonomy is slowly but surely slipping from them. Take a look at the Canada Year Book. In 1949 the division of public revenues was as follows: dominion government, 52 per cent; provincial governments, 27 per cent; municipal governments, 21 per cent. Look at it for the year 1956. It is as follows: dominion government, 72 per cent; provincial governments, 17 per cent; municipal governments, 11 per cent. There is a danger arising out of a continuation of that trend. The municipalities are the form of government closest to the people. They provide the facilities to 96698-12i
The Address-Mr. Irwin make life pleasant, but if their creators, the provinces, are to have their revenues absorbed by the dominion government to the extent indicated, then they are fighting a losing battle.
I find when I look at the question of the division of this revenue that the provincial governments are being hard put to it from year to year to make it their business to see that the municipalities receive the assistance they should get. The taxation on land values and improvements in order to provide revenue for the municipalities has gone just about as far as it can go as far as the owners of property are concerned, and I feel the time has come when the dominion government should make it its business to relinquish some of the hold it has on public revenues in this dominion and leave more of them available to the provinces so that the municipalities may be assisted in looking after the welfare of the people.
It would appear that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) feels that there should be some material difference between the policies pursued by the Liberal government and the one now in office. This group has been telling the public of this country for many years that there is no material difference between the two parties, and under the present circumstances the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition prove that assertion. If further proof is needed, it comes from the Prime Minister himself, for on at least two occasions during this session he has used the term, "since we came to power". If he had said, Mr. Speaker, "since we came to office", I would not have thought too much about it, I would not have commented upon it, but may I point out that the use of that word "power" has unfortunate implications. We have had some years of that already. Are we due for some more of the same? I hope not.
This government has my sympathy, Mr. Speaker, not because it is a minority government. That should not worry them too much, for so long as this government is prepared to bring down legislation that is in our opinion for the benefit of the Canadian people we will go along with it. We will help them out. In fact, we will help them out in more ways than that. We are prepared to step in and give them the benefit of our advice in these matters.

Well even that advice might be very valuable. So far as I am concerned, my sympathy is based on the fact that we as a country are merely getting a deal from a minor shuffle of the old deck of political

The Address-Mr. Rea
cards. We as a people want, not only a new deal, we want a completely new deck of cards. Furthermore we do not want the deuces wild and we want the jokers removed from the pack too.
The old line parties have nothing to offer but rehashes of outworn policies that bring no relief to the Canadian people as a whole. We have had 12 years of the Bretton Woods agreement, and its concomitant stupidities which have cost Canada her overseas markets. There is only one reason for production and that is consumption. Canada does not care where her consumers live. We have the capacity to produce goods and services away beyond our capacity to consume. Other peoples do not have the capacity to produce their actual needs.
Let us go back to section 91 of the British North America Act, take unto ourselves as a parliament the right to control and issue our own purchasing power and not strangle our economy by leaving that function in the hands of a private monopoly. My leader put forward a subamendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne and for the benefit of the house I want to repeat it. It is in these words:
That all the words in the amendment after the word "once" be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
''However, we regret that there is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that it is the government's intention to ask parliament to lay down a scientific, modern financial policy for Canada that will guide the Bank of Canada in its operations, bring about a speedy end to the present tight money policy, and effectively check the ever-rising cost of living."
The need of this country at the present time, Mr. Speaker, is to have the cost of living, which is rising at the rate of between 3 and 4 per cent a year, stabilized first of all and then slowly but surely reduced to the point where our dollar will resume a value that it has not had for the last 40 years. I appreciate the very close and kind attention I have received from the house and so far as I am concerned I will now take my seat.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to extend rather special congratulations to the Speaker because he happens to come from a riding right next to mine. I have known him for many years and have no hesitancy in going along with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, namely, that he will do an excellent job. To the Deputy Speaker I also offer my congratulations. While I am extending congratulations, I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder, (Mr. Arsenault) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

I am inclined to think that I am only echoing what has been said by other members when I say that because of the young men who have joined the Conservative ranks in the house our party is truly in a healthy position and this augurs well for the future of Canada. It is something of which we on this side of the house are very proud.
While talking about that, let me mention a couple of other things. Besides the people of various racial origins whom we have in the Conservative party and in the house, we have two ladies in the house, one of them the first cabinet lady in the history of the country. We have several Ukrainians, one who is a minister, and to complete the picture we have a Chinese member for the first time in Canadian history sitting in the House of Commons on the Conservative side. I think that speaks very well that the Conservative party is truly a Canadian and national party.
I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Landry). He spoke in glowing terms of the unity of the English and French speaking people of his riding and how by working together they became true Canadians. With that I fully agree. My mind also goes back to a speech made a couple of hours earlier today by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), one who has had a great deal more experience than the hon. member for Dorchester. The hon. member for Laurier made a speech that to my mind was strictly a propaganda speech designed to destroy the unity of Canada. I have never heard such a speech before. I am sure that Quebec wants to be treated as one of the ten provinces of Canada and not as a province that has to be treated in a special way.
When one of our members was speaking he asked the other side why they did not change their minds and make us go to the people and the answer was "We do not want to let you fellows off the hook." We know who is on the hook. Those who are afraid to fight are on the hook. Do not worry about us.
To come back to the speech from the throne, hon. members have all heard it or read it and the comments about it are excellent. One can only come to the conclusion that for the first time in 22 years a party that has been elected to form a government is starting right at the beginning to put every election promise into effect.

speechtext:
All you have to do is read the speech from the throne. Wait till the next one is brought down. It is going to be better. In

a country that is growing as fast as Canada and needs so many good people from various parts of the world I think we will all rejoice that the period it is necessary to live in Canada to qualify for the old age pension is going to be reduced. Just imagine what good news that will be for the older people who have come over here bringing with them their young people to contribute to the steady growth of our country. Their culture, which in many cases is hundreds and hundreds of years old, will eventually form part of what will be known as a Canadian culture. In this regard may I say I am sure the time will come when many people from what we now call the ethnic groups will be represented on the Canada council.
We have done a great deal, as have many other organizations, to try to help these newcomers to learn our language and understand our ways. I have often wondered whether those of us who were born here have ever tried to do our part in learning to understand the emotions and problems that have to be faced by these newcomers to our country. I am inclined to think that all of us should spend more time in this direction because while we are trying to teach these people our ways we are also being taught to understand their problems. It is only by this method that they will enter much faster into the various societies that Canada has to offer.
I also think that we are all trying sincerely to show these newcomers that we just have one class of citizenship in Canada, and that is first-class citizenship. The proposed legislation to decrease the length of time that one has to live here to qualify for the old age pension is something that will help to equalize all people in this country and it is certainly something which should have been done a long time ago by the do-nothing former Liberal government.
I shall just take a moment or two to speak about our senior citizens. We all know how long they tried to exist on the meagre allowance that was dealt out by the former government. Just before the election, of course, the government tried to bribe them with two extra cups of coffee each day. I should like to remind you of the proposal that has been made in the speech from the throne. I am sure these senior citizens are going to be very happy when this measure is actually implemented.
At this point I might say that there are no farmers in the Spadina riding, but we all know that if the farmers are successful then the remainder of the population in Canada is successful. We must operate as a team, and the suggested legislation will be of help to farmers in the future and therefore will be
The Address-Mr. Rea
appreciated not only by the farmers but by everyone else in Canada.
Some hon. members may have heard me talk some time ago about the deplorable situation in the electrical fixture business. For example, a manufacturer who manufactures electrical fixtures in Canada must manufacture them according to very high standards and rules. This is essential for the protection of human lives. Unfortunately certain fixtures can be imported from the United States which do not meet these high standards. Naturally, because the manufacturers do not have to use high class materials, these fixtures can be manufactured a great deal more cheaply and constitute not only unfair competition for the Canadian manufacturer but put the lives of everyone who uses them in danger. The loss from fires resulting from faulty electrical materials runs into many millions of dollars a year, and the loss of life of course is appalling. Those who were here, I believe it was two sessions ago, will remember what happened in Ottawa and will realize the seriousness of this situation.
You can have the best firefighting equipment in the world, the best trained firemen in the world, but when a person uses what we might call the "killer type" fixtures, firemen with all their equipment do not have a fair chance. Not long ago I bought a set of Christmas tree lights which had been imported from another country. The country of origin was not stamped on the box. I want to tell you that if I had ever connected those lights to a socket the whole thing would have gone up in flames. These lights were purchased in a reputable store, but I do not believe the purchasing agent realized the situation. I showed them to him and he immediately withdrew what he had left on the shelf. You will note I said, "what he had left". There had been some sold and goodness knows what happened as a result. Since being in power this government has actually started to ascertain what can be done about this matter. I am sure that before long they will correct another oversight of the "don't bother me" former government because I tried to get the former government to correct this situation. Evidently it was too much of a problem because the provinces had to be consulted and they did not want to take the time to do that.
On motion of Mr. Rea the debate was adjourned.
